doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Writing and arranging with Finale
summary: Raph describes how he writes and how Finale has cluttered and then clarified his arranging.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You said you’re still a morning person, even though you’re a musician.
Oh yeah. I’ve always been a morning person.
When you write are you a sit at the piano and write person?

Sometimes. It depends. If I’m composing I’m writing something truly original, very often I’ll sit at the piano. But if I’m arranging something it doesn’t really matter. I’ve gotten into Finale, using the computer and Finale and all of that and I’m just getting over the hurdle of being restricted, actually restricted by Finale, because things are so easy that you end up doubling things that you might not have doubled. You end up using sections of things that you might not have used if you were writing pen and ink. Finale is easy to take a whole section and stick it in later on, or to transpose something or to have something for one French horn and decide to stop it down for the second and third French horn also. It’s just so easy to do that sometimes, I think, I’m getting over the cluttering aspects of that.
Yeah, that’s interesting that you say that, how technology —
My writing prior to Finale was a little more transparent and it’s starting to get transparent again, which I kind of like.
Okay. Yeah. Let the machine do a little bit of the work for you.
Yeah. But I love it. I mean oh, not having to copy parts. That’s the whole ball game.
